narr: Welcome to the Introduction to Engineering course. In this study guide, we'll explore the foundational aspects of engineering, its economic impact, professional culture, and the ethical principles that guide the profession.
Let's start by understanding the broader role of engineering in society.

data.heading: The Economic Role of Engineering
bullets: Over 1.6 million engineers work in the United States
Engineering is the country's second-largest profession
Average starting salary: $68,000 per year (2017 data)
Engineering degree serves as a springboard to various fields
Engineering drives national development through infrastructure, industry, and technology

narr: Engineering plays a crucial economic role worldwide. In the United States alone, there are more than 1.6 million engineers, making it the country's second-largest profession.
The average starting salary for an engineering graduate in the US is $68,000 per year, according to 2017 data from NACE.
An engineering degree serves as a springboard, with graduates often moving into medicine, law, business, and public service.
Beyond individual careers, engineering serves as an engine of national development, building the infrastructure, industry, and technological base that drives economic growth.
According to Moaveni, citing U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data, the employment distribution among engineering specializations is as follows.
Civil engineering represents the largest field with 278,400 engineers, accounting for 17.7% of all engineers.
Mechanical engineering follows with 238,700 engineers (15.2%), while industrial engineering employs 214,800 engineers (13.7%).
Electrical engineering accounts for 157,800 engineers (10.0%).

data.heading: Culture, Identity and Professional Societies
bullets: The word 'engineer' is remarkably uniform across languages
Engineers typically work in teams of various sizes
Professional societies define standards, continuing education, and ethics
Key societies: ASME (mechanical), IEEE (electrical/computers), ASCE (civil), AIChE (chemical), AIAA (aerospace), ANS (nuclear)
Additional societies: ASTM (materials and testing), BMES (biomedical)

narr: The word 'engineer' is strikingly uniform across languages, reflecting a shared identity that transcends borders.
Engineers typically work in teams, ranging from two or three people to hundreds on large projects like passenger aircraft design.
Professional societies reinforce this shared identity by defining standards, continuing education requirements, and ethical guidelines for each discipline.

Key professional societies include ASME for mechanical engineers, IEEE for electrical and computer engineers, ASCE for civil engineers, AIChE for chemical engineers, AIAA for aerospace engineers, and ANS for nuclear engineers.
Additional societies mentioned include ASTM, which focuses on materials and testing, and BMES for biomedical engineering.

data.heading: The Ten Traits of the 'Problem-Solver DNA'

narr: These traits include being objective, analytical, creative, dedicated, curious, courageous, adventurous, enthusiastic, patient, and vigilant.
In the lab exercise, students select their trait, and groups are formed to ensure diverse combinations of these traits.
As the guide notes, 'a group of five Objective members will argue with itself forever and never solve anything', highlighting the importance of diversity in problem-solving teams.

data.heading: The Ten Traits of the 'Problem-Solver DNA' (cont.)

narr: The lecture and Lab 1 identify ten traits that constitute the 'problem-solver DNA' - the mindset of a good problem solver.
Engineers are fundamentally problem solvers with a firm command of fundamental principles.
They are analytical, attentive to detail, and creative, with a desire to learn throughout their lives.
They possess a portable core of knowledge, allowing them to work across different specializations.
Good engineers also excel in communication, time management, and interpersonal skills.
They are proficient in report writing, computer modeling, and active participation in professional organizations.
Finally, they thrive in team environments, collaborating effectively with colleagues.
Moaveni provides a parallel list of common traits among good engineers.

data.heading: Science — Engineering — Design: The Triad
bullets: Science: Investigates what exists, asks 'why?', seeks explanations and laws
Engineering: Creates what never existed, asks 'how?', applies scientific knowledge under constraints
Design: Creative act of giving form to solutions (shape, aesthetics, user experience)
Engineering design: Design disciplined by analysis (physics, materials, cost, manufacturability, safety)
Steve Jobs: 'Design is not how it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works'

narr: The week's content revolves around a triad: science, engineering, and design.
Science investigates what already exists, asking 'why does this happen?' and seeking explanations and generalizable laws about the natural world.
Engineering creates what has never existed, asking 'how do we make it work?' and applying scientific knowledge under real-world constraints.
Design is the creative, open-ended act of giving a solution its form, including shape, aesthetics, and user experience.
Engineering design is design disciplined by analysis, where physics, materials, cost, manufacturability, and safety constrain the possibilities.
As Steve Jobs famously said, 'Design is not how it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works'.

data.heading: The Connection Scheme
bullets: Engineering draws on science and expresses itself through design

narr: These three elements are interconnected in a specific way.
Science provides the understanding of the natural world.
Design shapes creative solutions to problems.
Engineering builds working solutions that function in the real world.
Engineering draws upon scientific knowledge and expresses itself through the creative process of design.

data.title: Week 1 Ethics
data.subtitle: The NSPE Codes and Personal Ethics

narr: Now let's turn to the central theme of week 1: ethics. This encompasses the lecture, all of Lab 1, and material from Kosky chapter 1 and Moaveni chapter 5.
We'll explore professional codes of ethics, focusing on the NSPE codes and the importance of personal ethics in engineering practice.

data.heading: Professional Code of Ethics
bullets: Ensures the profession serves legitimate purposes of all stakeholders
Protects members from consequences of competition
Allows freedom to enjoy desirable consequences: invention and innovation
Provides a framework for ethical decision-making
Empowers engineers to resist pressure: 'As a professional, I cannot ethically place business interests above professional ethics'

narr: A professional code of ethics aims to ensure that the engineering profession serves the legitimate purposes of all stakeholders: oneself, the employer, the profession, and society.
The code protects engineers from the unwanted consequences of competition, such as the pressure to 'cut corners' for the sake of savings.
At the same time, it leaves engineers free to enjoy the desirable consequences of their profession: invention and innovation.
The code provides a framework for ethical decision-making in complex situations.
Armed with the code, an engineer can resist inappropriate pressure with the phrase: 'As a professional, I cannot ethically place business interests above professional ethics'.

data.heading: The Fundamental Canons of the NSPE
bullets: Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public
Perform services only in areas of their competence
Issue public statements only in an objective and truthful manner
Act for each employer or client as faithful agents or trustees
Conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully

narr: The National Society of Professional Engineers (NSPE) has established fundamental canons that engineers must follow in their professional duties.
First, engineers must hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public.
Second, they should perform services only in areas of their competence.
Third, when issuing public statements, engineers must be objective and truthful.
Fourth, engineers must act as faithful agents or trustees for each employer or client.
Fifth, they must avoid deceptive acts in their professional practice.
Finally, engineers must conduct themselves honorably, responsibly, ethically, and lawfully to enhance the honor, reputation, and usefulness of the profession.
